- E2E tracing
  - ML Ops: Limited need — logging and experiment tracking record runs and metrics, but not full per-input trace of internal steps.
  - LLM Ops: Essential and heavyweight — you must trace the entire journey of every input (retrieval, augmentation, model generation) to diagnose failure modes, reproduce outputs, compute fine-grained metrics, and decide remediation (often fix app rather than retrain).

- Guardrails
  - ML Ops: Usually unnecessary — deterministic numeric outputs have little risk of toxicity, PII leakage, or “hijacking,” so simple safeguards suffice.
  - LLM Ops: Mandatory — free-text generation can produce toxicity, PII, or be exploited; guardrails are required to constrain behavior, filter outputs, and keep the application safe. Evaluations must include safety, fidelity, and policy compliance checks.

- RAG pipeline (retrieval → augmentation → generation)
  - ML Ops: Not applicable in classic pipelines; evaluation focuses on model metrics on labeled rows.
  - LLM Ops: Changes what you evaluate and track — experiment tracking must lock documents used, chunk strategy/overlap, embedding model, providers, etc., because those artifacts drive output. RAG makes evaluation workflow-driven: you must test retrieval accuracy, augmentation correctness, generation alignment, and end-to-end reproducibility.

Bottom line: ML Ops evaluations are simple, numeric, and batch-oriented; LLM Ops evaluations are workflow-driven, dynamic, and heavyweight — they require streaming-aware serving, full E2E tracing, guardrails, and strict artifact/experiment tracking (especially for RAG) to reliably evaluate and operate systems."

  - Role: break long documents into logical chunks (e.g., 10‑min transcript pieces) for downstream processing.

  - Persistence: chunks can be persisted (recommended) to avoid re-splitting on repeated runs.
  - Compute/Cost: minimal CPU; cheap compared with embedding.

- Embedder
  - Role: convert each chunk to a semantic numeric representation (vectors) that capture meaning.
  - I → O: chunk text → embedding vectors (usually via external model/API).
  - Persistence: embeddings should be saved (don’t re‑compute each query).
  - Compute/Cost: high — uses model compute and/or paid API calls; main cost driver in ingestion.

- VecDB + metadata
  - Role: persist embeddings and associated metadata (original chunk text, source, timestamps) and serve similarity retrieval.
  - I → O: vectors + metadata → stored index; queries → retrieved nearest vectors + their metadata/original text.
  - Persistence: primary persistent store for retrieval; stores vectors and the grounding data needed to produce grounded answers.
  - Compute/Cost: storage & indexing cost; similarity search cost (much cheaper than repeated embedding calls). By storing embeddings+metadata you avoid repeated expensive embedder calls and keep responses grounded to course transcripts.

Key operational note: keep embeddings and original chunk text (metadata) in the VecDB to ground answers and avoid re‑embedding (major cost savings). DocLoader/Chunker are cheap I/O/CPU steps; Embedder is the costly, compute‑heavy step to minimize and persist."
